films.ex: My movie project for 2026 is to watch a documentary a week. I started off with this movie and I think I can safely say I won't see another movie like it this year (or ever). It is literally unlike anything I've ever seen -- I sat there with my jaw dropped for the first 30 minutes of it. The…
films.desc: Former Indonesian death-squad leaders who took part in the 1965 mass killings agree to re-enact their crimes on camera, staging them as scenes in gangster, western, and musical movies of their own design.

films.ex: A standard documentary that highlights the heroic, courageous work done by the women of the news organization Khabar Laharia in Uttar Pradesh, India. It makes up for a lack of interesting form and style by providing us a look at the ridiculous and dangerous attitudes of men (in general) and Modhi's…
films.desc: Follows the reporters of Khabar Lahariya, a news outlet run by Dalit women in India, over about five years as they move from print to smartphone-based digital journalism.

films.ex: A very interesting look at a ridiculous endurance race that includes some insightful thoughts on the nature of competition, goals, and finding your own limits. Also, the guy who runs it is an absolute boss. I have tons of respect for all the people who attempt this race -- except that one (white…
films.desc: A look at the Barkley Marathons, a secretive and brutally difficult trail race in a small Tennessee town, and the runners who try it. Entry is by a hidden application process, the start time is unannounced, and the course changes every year.

films.ex: The courage Gena has to flout convention in Russia (and not just Russia, but hell-and-gone former gulag Russia) is astounding. She exists in a place where literally at any moment she could be apprehended and disappeared simply for being who they are, and still they persist despite having no one on…
films.desc: Follows Gena Marvin, a young queer artist from Magadan who stages costumed street performances in Moscow to challenge ideas of beauty and queerness and to protest the harassment of LGBTIQ+ people.

films.ex: Less about the actual apartment per se -- although how they discovered the space, furnished it, and kept it secret was fascinating -- and more about what it represented: the fight against commercialism and gentrification and the importance of art for art's sake.
films.desc: Eight young people from Rhode Island secretly built and lived in a hidden apartment inside the Providence Place mall from 2003 to 2007. The film begins as a prank story and grows into questions about art and activism.

films.ex: This was fine - an interesting story told competently. Lynsey Addario is a fucking boss.
films.desc: A portrait of Pulitzer Prize-winning photojournalist Lynsey Addario and her career photographing conflict, including the personal cost of the work: two kidnappings and long stretches away from her husband and sons.

films.ex: Fun
films.desc: The story of the college all-star squad brought in to scrimmage the 1992 U.S. Olympic Dream Team, with players including Grant Hill, Chris Webber, and Penny Hardaway, and the upset win that shaped the team's run to gold.

films.ex: This was fine, broke no new ground but wow that was a hell of a year at the movies.
films.desc: Morgan Neville's essay film on 1975, a year of social and political turmoil, seen through the movies and culture it produced.

films.ex: Competent and held my attention, which sounds like a backhanded compliment but isn't. Everyone involved seems to be at exactly the right level of seriousness for an MTV documentary about a genre of music from 40+ years ago that wasn't even a genre at the time. My biggest takeaway was how…
films.desc: An HBO Music Box documentary on the late-1970s and early-1980s West Coast soft rock known as yacht rock, with artists including Christopher Cross, Michael McDonald, Kenny Loggins, Steely Dan, and Toto, and how a style once mocked earned a respected place in music history.

films.ex: Heroic and heartbreaking, maddening and amazing
films.desc: Filmmakers Andrew Jarecki and Charlotte Kaufman investigate Alabama's prison system. A 2019 visit to film a revival meeting turned into a six-year inquiry after incarcerated men privately warned them about hidden abuses.

films.ex: I knew about the Found Footage Festival, though I've never seen it, but had no idea about the guys behind it. This doc presents a typical backstory -- goofs and pranksters as kids who found a way to turn their interests into their career (such as it is) -- but also digs into the real-life problems…
films.desc: Follows Joe Pickett and Nick Prueher, the pranksters behind the Found Footage Festival, a live show built from obscure and bizarre VHS tapes. On a nationwide tour, the film shows how their pranks and legal pressure strain a long friendship.

films.ex: This is the story of four incredibly talented musicians who played on some of the best music of the last 50 years, and they still get together and play and talk about stuff. It's all vibes and amazing skill and Phil Collins. WIYL Adult Album Alternative, non-toxic male friendship, guys named Rusty…
films.desc: Denny Tedesco's film about a group of session musicians, among them bassist Leland Sklar, drummer Russ Kunkel, and guitarists Waddy Wachtel, Steve Postel, and Danny Kortchmar, and their work during the 1970s singer-songwriter boom, told through interviews with them and well-known artists.

films.ex: (Not sure if I'm going to count this one or not because it was a DNF.) The best Errol Morris movies, IMO, are the ones where he can just sort of turn on his camera and let his subject be weird, or compelling, or evil. The residents of Vernon, Florida. Hawking. McNamara. Rumsfeld. Bannon. Huh, maybe…
films.desc: Errol Morris interviews spy novelist John le Carré (David Cornwell) in what was meant to be his last and most personal interview. It covers six decades of his life and how his con-man father shaped his writing, with archival footage.

films.ex: Much like Queendom, this is the story of one person's resistance to Vladimir Putin leading up to and immediately after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. In that case it was a queer drag performer in the ass-end of Russia; in this case it's an event coordinator at a primary school in a different ass-end…
films.desc: A Russian teacher secretly films his small-town school as it turns into a military recruitment hub during Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and the moral bind he faces as propaganda and militarism grow around him.

films.t: Come See Me in the Good Light
films.ex: When someone you love dies, it's normal to see them in everything around you. Even with that, though, watching a movie about someone doing aggressive chemo to fight their metastatic cancer a week after your father died from the aggressive chemo he was doing to fight his metastatic cancer is a bit…
films.desc: Ryan White's film follows poets Andrea Gibson and Megan Falley as they look back on their lives, their art, and their romance while Gibson lives with a serious illness, and shows how limited time changes a relationship.

films.t: Listers: A Glimpse Into Extreme Birdwatching
films.ex: In which two brothers from Missouri get high and decide to drive around the country and attempt a "Big Year," which is trying to see as many different types of birds as they can in a calendar year. Does it surprise you that people do that? It shouldn't -- people are weird and magical. These guys…
films.desc: Brothers Owen and Quentin Reiser try to spot as many bird species as possible across the contiguous United States in 2024, an extreme form of birdwatching called a big year, traveling by minivan and facing harsh conditions.

films.ex: Uplifting but also raises a lot of moral questions, many of which the artist seemed uninterested in addressing. His heart was absolutely in the right place and he definitely felt a kinship with the pickers but it seemed like he still couldn't help but be patronizing. Still, he raised many thousands…
films.desc: Artist Vik Muniz returns to his native Brazil to work at Jardim Gramacho, a huge garbage dump near Rio, and photographs the workers who collect recyclables there. The film shows both their dignity and their hardships as they imagine new futures.

films.ex: These people are fucking insane.
films.desc: Climbers Jimmy Chin, Conrad Anker, and Renan Ozturk make a second attempt on Mount Meru, a steep, difficult peak in India, after a near-fatal failed try in 2008. Short on supplies and facing brutal weather, they have to rely on one another to survive.

films.ex: Hurt people hurt people, but sometimes they manage not to. A look at three kids growing up in various bad situations and the ways they cope (or don't).
films.desc: Filmmaker Bing Liu recorded three young men, bound by skateboarding and a wish to escape turbulent homes, over roughly twelve years. The film looks at difficult childhoods, poverty, modern masculinity, and how abuse can pass between generations.

films.ex: The producer would have made a really good Nazi prison guard.
films.desc: Clair Titley's film about Tomoaki Hamatsu, the Japanese comedian known as Nasubi, who starred in the late-1990s reality show A Life in Prizes. He lived in isolation, unclothed, relying on whatever he could win through mail-in coupons, and the film draws on interviews about his family, childhood, and later life.

films.ex: This was so much more heartfelt and insightful than I expected it to be. It combines interviews with some of the best-known "clones" (Bruce Li, Bruce Le, Bruce Leung, Dragon Lee), actors (Roy Horan, Ron van Clief, Mars), directors like Godfrey Ho, and Golden Harvest producer André Morgan…
films.desc: David Gregory's documentary on the low-budget films that exploited Bruce Lee's fame after his death. It uses archival footage and focuses on the look-alike performers who kept his on-screen image alive.

films.ex: There is a scene in this movie where the husband (but NOT the wife) and another guy take an inflatable boat out onto a lake of acid and once the acid eats through the steel cable on their equipment they decide to bail but it takes them THREE HOURS to get back to shore and then he quotes Nietzsche…
films.desc: Sara Dosa's documentary about Katia and Maurice Krafft, a French volcanologist couple who spent two decades traveling the world to study and film eruptions. It is built largely from their own footage and follows their story through their deaths in a 1991 volcanic explosion.

films.ex: First 30: So is this guy just a monster? Middle 30: Hmm, maybe something is weird about this family ... Last 30: Nope, definitely a monster.
films.desc: Bart Layton's documentary about Frédéric Bourdin, who posed as Nicholas Barclay, a Texas boy who disappeared at 13. It mixes reenactments, interviews, and real documents to examine how the Barclay family accepted a returning son who looked and sounded strikingly different.

films.t: What the Hell Happened to Blood, Sweat & Tears?
films.ex: They got fucked by the US government, that's what.
films.desc: John Scheinfeld's film about Blood, Sweat & Tears and their 1970 State Department-sponsored tour of Eastern Bloc countries. It argues the tour damaged the band's reputation with American fans, who saw them as government puppets, and that the band was pressured into going so singer David Clayton-Thomas could get a green card.

films.ex: When I watched Bojack Horseman I remember thinking how crazy it was that the best representation of depression I'd ever seen was in a cartoon about a talking horse. I can now add to that how crazy it is that the best exploration of the need for human interaction and art I've ever seen is in…
films.desc: Stranded during the COVID-19 lockdown, actors Sam Crane and Mark Oosterveen stage Shakespeare's Hamlet inside Grand Theft Auto and film it. The production plays out in the game's virtual Los Santos, setting Hamlet's dilemma amid violence and vulnerability.

films.t: Mountain Queen: The Summits of Lhakpa Sherpa
films.ex: Alex Honnold could never. Any of it.
films.desc: Follows Lhakpa Sherpa, a Nepali-born mountaineer who works as a dishwasher in Connecticut while preparing for a tenth Everest summit that would set a record for female climbers. It also portrays her life as an immigrant, a single mother of two teenage daughters, and a survivor of spousal abuse.

films.ex: A bunch of Hall of Famers sitting around talking about which pitchers threw the fastest? I could watch eight hours of this shit.
films.desc: Narrated by Kevin Costner, a look at the science and psychology of pitching and hitting, centered on the fraction of a second a fast pitch takes to reach the plate, with current and former players and scientists.

films.ex: The thing GenX is best at is the ability to be both ironic and sincere at the same time.
films.desc: Alex Ross Perry's experimental film about the indie band Pavement, mixing documentary footage, scripted comedy, a stage musical built from their songs, and a museum exhibit about the group. It follows Perry's struggle to pull the project together as the frontman hesitates and the lead actor starts sounding and acting like him off set.

films.ex: A straightforward look at how the greed of medical device companies combined with a complete lack of oversight by the FDA has led to thousands of people (mostly women -- go figure) dying, becoming disabled, and/or experiencing severe chronic pain. The best thing this movie does is get out of the…
films.desc: Kirby Dick and Amy Ziering's documentary on the American medical device industry and how weak oversight, corporate concealment, and profit motives can put patients at risk. It follows people whose lives were permanently damaged by devices meant to help them.

films.ex: I was aware of only the barest outline of what happened at Attica -- there was a riot, and some prisoners died -- but watching this movie felt like watching a horror movie that you already know the plot of. I knew what was going to happen; the question was how. The answer? Nothing that happened at…
films.desc: Stanley Nelson's documentary on the rising hostility between incarcerated people and guards at Attica Correctional Facility in 1971, building to the September 9 uprising, one of the largest prison riots in American history.

films.ex: I wanted to be cynical about this guy and his parasocial relationship with this pangolin, but the truth is he's just a guy who was casting around for something to hold onto in his life and happened on pangolins. The fact that this movie was as much, if not more, about him than about the pangolin…
films.desc: Pippa Ehrlich's film follows South African volunteer Gareth Thomas as he rescues Kulu, a baby pangolin, an endangered and heavily trafficked animal, and spends six months rehabilitating it so it can return to the wild.

films.ex: Enthusiastic but amateurish.
films.desc: Matt Flesch's documentary looks back on the 1990 Chicago White Sox season, the team's last at Comiskey Park, through archival footage and interviews with players, coaches, stadium staff, and fans. A team expected to finish last unexpectedly chases the Oakland Athletics.

films.ex: Charming and insightful. Varda examines gleaning (or salvaging, which is different, as her berobed lawyers standing in the fields and on street corners will tell you) from multiple angles. For some it is a survival tool, for others a revolt against capitalism, for still others an inspiration for…
films.desc: Agnès Varda's documentary about people who gather leftover produce from fields after the harvest and others who salvage usable food at Paris markets, whether from need or to cut waste, treating them as people who find value in what society throws away.

films.ex: The stories these players tell just kick you right in the heart. Growing up and being continually told, through word and deed, that you don't belong, is something I can't imagine, and I'm so glad they took the time to talk about how it affected them. The courage that they have (that they shouldn't…
films.desc: Hubert Davis's documentary on the history of anti-Black racism in hockey, from segregated leagues in the 19th century to today's NHL, where Black players still face bigotry. P.K. Subban, Akim Aliu, and Sarah Nurse are among the players in the cast.

films.ex: Really good but I wanted it to be great. Strangely I think it would have benefitted from some non-player talking heads who could have given more context.
films.desc: About the unofficial 1971 Women's World Cup, a tournament that drew large crowds but has been left out of sporting history, told through the accounts of the women who played in it.

films.t: The Last Guest of the Holloway Motel
films.ex: As a guy sliding inexorably toward oldness I'm glad to see examples of people continuing to change and grow no matter their age. Tony Powell has had a hell of a life and seemed (at least outwardly) to be fine with the good and bad of it. Doing this documentary seemed to force him to deal with…
films.desc: Follows Tony Powell, a former British footballer who now manages a struggling motel in Hollywood, and through his reflections explores a lonely life and the road he never chose.

films.ex: OK. Lots of thoughts about this one. A (white) guy born with the spirit of wanderlust decides to re-enact a trip to Patagonia that a previous generation of (white) guys born with the spirit of wanderlust undertook in the '60s. Along the way he has his eyes opened to the plight of indigenous peoples…
films.desc: Chris Malloy's documentary follows climber and surfer Jeff Johnson as he sails down South America's Pacific coast toward Patagonia, retracing a 1968 journey by Yvon Chouinard and Doug Tompkins. Conservation is a central theme, and the film ends with his unfinished attempt to climb the Corcovado volcano.

films.ex: You let your camera lead you to odd and interesting places, you're not afraid to make yourself look silly for a laugh, and you never pass up an opportunity for a butt joke. (Also, a bunch of the negative reviews I read here accuse Wilson of making fun of the people he talks to, but I didn't see…
films.desc: John Wilson sets out to make a documentary about concrete, the world's most widely used building material, after taking a workshop on writing Hallmark movies, and applies that formula to the film. The project's struggles reflect the tension between artistic freedom and the demands of the film industry.

films.ex: I felt a little bit bait-and-switched with this one. I went in expecting an in-depth look at Stokes' tape collection, with insight into why she did it and what it meant and means. The movie gives some of that, but it's much more focused on Stokes herself. Fortunately, she is fascinating and…
films.desc: Matt Wolf's documentary about Marion Stokes, a secretive activist who taped television broadcasts nonstop from 1979 to 2012 and built a collection of roughly 70,000 VHS tapes, and what her recordings preserve about the news and events of those decades.

films.t: Imagining the Indian: The Fight Against Native American Mascoting
films.ex: Well-made and straightforward documentary about the use of Indian words and imagery by sports teams. I didn't really learn anything new in that area, but Suzan Shown Harjo is a main focus of the movie and I knew nothing about her, so getting to learn about what she's done throughout her life as an…
films.desc: Aviva Kempner and Ben West's documentary on the movement to remove Native American team names, mascots, images, and gestures that many Native people and their allies consider offensive. It uses archival footage and interviews, and covers teams such as Kansas City's football team and Atlanta's baseball team that have resisted changing their names.

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's film, produced by The Guardian, which its festival listing describes as an examination of the systems behind Israel's planned mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. It was shot at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv.

Kahlil Joseph's hybrid film blending documentary, visual essay, and speculative fiction. It builds on W.E.B. Du Bois's unfinished Encyclopedia Africana project and recasts the news broadcast as an alternative archive, treating history as an ongoing force in contemporary Black life.

Recounts a 2021 standoff on a Glasgow street, where neighbors and activists gathered to block an immigration van detaining two local residents, alongside the earlier stories and history that shaped the community.

An archive-based documentary about the making of The Day After (1983), the made-for-TV movie about nuclear war. It looks at the commercial network that produced it, its audience of over 100 million viewers, and how the broadcast pushed the U.S. president to address nuclear weapons.

Alex Ross Perry's documentary, narrated by Maya Hawke, charts the history of video rental stores from the late 1970s to their near-disappearance in the 2010s. Built from hundreds of film and TV clips, it follows no single person and draws on Daniel Herbert's book and Perry's own time working in a New York shop.

A 2024 documentary by Basel Adra, Hamdan Ballal, Yuval Abraham, and Rachel Szor on the displacement of residents in Masafer Yatta in the West Bank. It follows Palestinian activist Basel and Israeli journalist Yuval as their friendship grows while they film the demolition of villagers' homes, which are rebuilt and destroyed again after a 22-year court case.

Poh Si Teng's documentary about three American physicians, one Palestinian, one Jewish, and one Zoroastrian, who volunteer in besieged Gaza hospitals, then return to the U.S. and campaign, including in Congress, for the patients and colleagues they left behind.

An Oscar-nominated documentary on the 1960 Congolese coup and the assassination of Patrice Lumumba. It uses archival footage and jazz to show how American cultural and political involvement shaped events, including the Cold War strategy of sending musicians like Thelonious Monk and Max Roach abroad, set against Congolese resistance.
Ceyda Torun's documentary about the stray cats of Istanbul, the people who look after them, and how the city is changing.

films.t: The Kingdom of Dreams and Madness
films.desc: A 2013 documentary on the creative process at Studio Ghibli, centered on Hayao Miyazaki as he prepares The Wind Rises, then planned as his last feature. It also follows his mentor and rival Isao Takahata as he slowly finishes The Tale of the Princess Kaguya, with producer Toshio Suzuki managing both releases.

A hand-drawn animated documentary in a vivid comic-book style. Director Ari Folman has lost his memories of serving as a young soldier in Lebanon in the 1980s, and seeks out former comrades and specialists to recover them, confronting the 1982 Sabra and Shatila massacres.

Stanley Nelson and Valerie Scoon's Hulu documentary on the tense and often hostile relationship between African Americans and the police, from the origins of Southern police forces during slavery, through mob violence after the Great Migration, to recent high-profile cases and current efforts to address the conflict.
Michael Apted's ninth film in the Up series, checking in on a group of British-born adults after a seven-year gap as they reflect on how their lives have changed.

Follows Florida's yearly public contest in which amateur hunters compete to remove invasive pythons from the Everglades. Over ten nights, a colorful group of participants take on hazardous wetland terrain, nocturnal wildlife, and their own motives for a $10,000 top prize.

Filmmaker Ahsen Nadeem, a Muslim going through a crisis of faith, visits an isolated Buddhist monastery in Japan looking for answers. He befriends a monk who says he would rather eat ice cream and listen to heavy metal than meditate, and their conversations explore faith and worldly desire.

The story of Chol Soo Lee, a man falsely convicted of a murder in San Francisco, and the 1970s grassroots campaign in which activists and the Asian American community rallied to win his freedom, told through archival footage and interviews.

A documentary about Bob Uecker, the longtime Milwaukee Brewers broadcaster, covering his career in baseball, in the broadcast booth, and on screen. Directed by Michael Vollmann and Steve Farr, it focuses on his final seasons calling Brewers games, which they followed for roughly two years.

A 40-minute showcase of short documentaries by Chicago-based filmmakers on federal immigration enforcement, including ICE, and its impact on communities, centered on Operation Midway Blitz in Chicago. The works include personal testimonies, a documentary about a DHS visit to a Chicago job fair, and bodycam footage of a violent confrontation in Albany Park.

Follows Phil Demers, a former animal trainer at MarineLand in Niagara Falls who became a whistleblower alleging animal abuse and campaigned to end marine mammal captivity. It also covers his bond with a walrus named Smooshi and the lawsuit and custody battle that followed.

Doug Liman's first feature-length documentary examines the 2018 sexual assault allegations against Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. It draws on leaked text messages, interviews with high school and Yale classmates and with journalists who covered the case, and a new interview with accuser Debbie Ramirez, with Christine Blasey Ford appearing in the opening scene.

John Scheinfeld's documentary, based on a book by John Sexton, treats baseball as a source of spiritual meaning rather than only a sport. Drawing on the ideas of religious historian Mircea Eliade, it argues that the ballpark and its rituals can connect fans to something transcendent, with interviews with former players, a manager, and religion scholars.

Kim A. Snyder's documentary about librarians who band together to push back against book bans and protect intellectual freedom. It focuses on educators confronting censorship in states like Texas and Florida, including Suzette Baker and Becky Calzada.

A documentary about the 1994 U.S. Men's National Soccer Team as it prepared for the World Cup with no professional league, little star power, and scarce funding. It mixes new interviews with the team's own 1990s camcorder footage.

Grace Hughes-Hallett's documentary follows 19-year-old Kristi, who learns from her medical records that the doctor and parents she trusted had hidden a central truth about her body. Her search leads to a discredited 1970s psychology experiment that justified unnecessary childhood surgeries, and the film uses archival material, testimony, and expert commentary to examine the harm done to intersex people.

Vera Drew's 2022 superhero parody that unofficially spoofs Batman characters. It follows a transgender woman inspired by the Joker who grows up dreaming of stand-up comedy, forms an anti-comedy troupe in Gotham City, and comes into her own identity.

Peter McDowell investigates the death of his eldest brother Jim, a Vietnam veteran who died in 1972 in Saigon, where he was living as a civilian. He pieces it together from hundreds of Jim's letters, interviews with family and friends, and his search across the United States, Vietnam, and France, touching on grief and family secrets.

Soraya Simi's documentary follows Angela Madsen, a former Marine, three-time Paralympian, and ocean rower, through the year before her solo, unsupported row from Los Angeles to Hawaii. It mixes her love story with her wife, Debra, and her athletic determination, until the film team and Debra lose contact with her at sea.

Danny Abel's documentary follows Jeremiah Heaton, an American who in 2014 claimed 500,000 acres of desert between Egypt and Sudan, first to make his daughter a princess and later to build an actual nation. It traces the media attention, a Disney movie deal, and his push for government and political connections.

Tracy Droz Tragos and Andrew Droz Palermo's 2014 documentary follows three teenage boys coming of age in a struggling small town in Missouri. Through their families' struggles with poverty, addiction, and incarceration, it also captures the rhythms and beauty of rural community life.

David Osit's film revisits To Catch a Predator, the hidden-camera series that aired on Dateline from 2004 to 2007 and staged stings on men who believed they were meeting minors. It questions the ethics of true crime entertainment and the public appetite for punishment and shaming.

A PBS Independent Lens documentary directed by Stanley Nelson that traces the history and influence of funk, the danceable blend of R&B, gospel, jazz, and blues rooted in Black culture. It follows the genre from the Motown era through James Brown and George Clinton's Parliament-Funkadelic, using musician interviews.

A Peacock true crime documentary produced by Rachel Maddow about a standoff between the sheriff's department in Idabel, Oklahoma, and the Willingham family, who run the local newspaper, the McCurtain Gazette. It follows the family's fight for press freedom after they reported alleged misconduct in the sheriff's office, including claims that officers discussed having them killed.

Andres Veiel's 2024 documentary takes a critical look at filmmaker Leni Riefenstahl, from her celebrated Nazi-era films to her final years. Drawing on her personal archive of home movies, letters, and private conversations, it tests whether she was an apolitical artist or knowingly used her talent in service of fascist ideology.

A 2025 documentary directed by Rob Petit that follows explorers into hard-to-reach places such as caves, flooded drains, and underground laboratories. Narrated by Sandra Hüller, it reveals the hidden worlds beneath our feet and invites reflection on humanity's modest place on Earth.

A reenactment-style film shot inside a theater in Montreuil about the Paris Commune of March 1871. It alternates a soothing Versailles TV report with a community access channel run by the insurgents, and about 220 mostly amateur actors play Popincourt workers debating issues that speak as much to today's unemployment and racism as to 1871, arguing for ethical commitment and participatory democracy.

Amy Berg's documentary portrait of the singer best known for his cover of "Hallelujah" and his 1994 debut album Grace. It follows his bandmates and the women who knew him best, using archival footage, voicemails, and notebook excerpts to present him as a vibrant, talented artist rather than only a tragic figure.

A documentary about Tangier Island, a historic fishing community in Virginia's Chesapeake Bay, as erosion and environmental change threaten its future. It quietly observes residents' daily work, worship, and family life and how they are adapting, rather than focusing on policy debates or expert commentary.

A 2026 Australian experimental documentary by debut filmmaker Josef Gatti, who uses scientific experiments to reveal hidden natural forces, such as soap bubbles that resemble distant planets and ferrofluids that seem to move with life. Inspired by his physics-teacher father, Gatti performs the experiments himself and captures everything in camera without visual effects.

films.t: The Pink Pill: Sex, Drugs and Who Has Control
films.desc: Follows advocates campaigning for FDA approval of a drug shown to increase women's sexual desire. The film argues that medicine and medical education overlook women's sexual health, even as many drugs are developed for men's erectile dysfunction.

Follows Hatidze, a woman in the mountains of Macedonia who cares for her ailing mother while earning a living harvesting honey with age-old beekeeping methods. Her solitude is disrupted when a boisterous family moves in next door and also takes up beekeeping, turning a welcome presence into a source of friction.

Jehane Noujaim's documentary follows a group of Egyptian activists who risk their lives confronting regimes and military forces during the country's revolution, from the 2011 overthrow of a 30-year dictatorship onward, and through the 2013 removal of a second president in three years. It offers an immersive, on-the-ground view of the upheaval.

Daniel Lindsay and T.J. Martin's 2011 documentary about a high school football team in an under-resourced part of Memphis, Tennessee. It follows three young players and their volunteer coach, Bill Courtney, as they face hardships off the field alongside the season's games.
Charles Ferguson's 2007 American documentary examines how the Bush administration handled the Iraq War and the occupation that followed.

Kirby Dick's 2015 documentary examines sexual assault at American colleges and how schools may have concealed it, focusing on the harm to students and their families. It comes from the team behind The Invisible War.

Follows Indian journalist Ravish Kumar over two years as he works in a newsroom under pressure from fake news, shrinking ratings, and budget cuts. It asks whether audiences still want fact-based reporting or whether his show will be overtaken by sensationalism and ratings-driven decisions.

films.t: They'll Love Me When I'm Dead
films.desc: Morgan Neville's documentary examines Orson Welles's last years and his fixation on finishing The Other Side of the Wind, a film he never completed despite years of work. It combines previously unseen footage of Welles on set with new interviews with the film's cast and crew.

Gabriela Cowperthwaite's 2022 documentary examines how governments and private investors compete for control of the world's food and water supplies. It follows investigative reporters from the Center for Investigative Reporting as they connect local disputes, such as water shortages in Arizona and displaced communities in Zambia, to larger geopolitical deals, including China's purchase of Smithfield Foods.

Follows members of the Sugarcane Reserve in Canada as they investigate child disappearances and abuse at a nearby Catholic-run residential school. Their search prompts a broader community reckoning, with survivors sharing painful memories while police and suspects are shown to be unhelpful.

A profile of journalist Amy Goodman, from her upbringing in a rabbi's family to decades of reporting from conflict zones and the Democracy Now! newsroom. It explores the value and risks of independent journalism amid corporate consolidation and political pressure, and how her team's grassroots broadcast offers alternative viewpoints.

A 2024 documentary directed by James Jones about the personal cost of opposing Vladimir Putin and exposing the truth about modern Russia. It follows three people: an insider from Russia's poisoning program trying to escape, an activist who survived two poisonings and now faces treason charges, and a man exposing the program who has been forced into hiding.

Omar Majeed and Peter Mishara's documentary traces disco's deep roots, its harsh backlash, and its lasting influence on later music. It is told largely through the recollections of Chic founder Nile Rodgers and New York DJ Nicky Siano, with archival footage of underground clubs showing the era's culture from the inside.

Follows the small town of Marion, Kansas, after police raided the local newspaper, the Marion County Record, and its 98-year-old co-owner died, drawing national and international attention. The film explores the resulting debate over government overreach, press ethics, the future of small-town news, and constitutional rights.

A 2021 documentary directed by Gorman Bechard and Fred Uhter about the life of musician Jay Bennett, best known for his work with the band Wilco. It is Bechard's sixth rock documentary, and reviewers have credited it with a close, detailed look at Bennett's talent and his contributions to Wilco's music.

A team of Ukrainian journalists working for The Associated Press is trapped in the besieged city of Mariupol, recording Russian atrocities as the only international reporters still there. Drawing on director Mstyslav Chernov's own news reports and personal footage, the film shows civilians suffering under the siege and what it takes to report from a war zone.

Mstyslav Chernov's documentary follows Ukrainian troops as they push through a mined forest toward Andriivka, a village occupied by Russian forces, to try to retake it. It focuses on soldiers such as Fedya, who leads the advance, balancing their personal stories and everyday camaraderie with the combat and deaths they face.

An animated documentary by Jonas Poher Rasmussen about Amin Nawabi, a 36-year-old scholar who has concealed his childhood escape from Afghanistan as a refugee for two decades. It blends a story of coming out and self-discovery with a look at the refugee experience, as his buried past threatens the life he is building with his future husband.

Follows Sara Shahverdi, a 37-year-old former midwife who has just become the first elected councilwoman in her remote northwest Iranian village. She works to end patriarchal customs by teaching teenage girls to ride motorcycles and stopping child marriages, and the film shows her determined efforts when her motives are questioned.

Morgan Neville's 2011 documentary about the early-1970s singer-songwriter scene centered on Doug Weston's Troubadour club in West Hollywood. Using archival footage, rare performances, and interviews with artists such as James Taylor, Carole King, and Joni Mitchell, it traces the scene's rise and eventual decline.

films.t: Respect Yourself: The Stax Records Story
films.desc: Traces the founding of Stax Records and its role in developing soul music and the Memphis sound. It features classic performances and interviews with founder Jim Stewart and Stax artists, and shows how the label, racially integrated during segregation, grew into one of the nation's most successful Black-owned companies.

Traces how baseball has changed over time, from early ballparks to the present, through the paintings of Dick Perez, the Baseball Hall of Fame's longtime official artist. It also connects the sport's evolution to Perez's own story as an immigrant.

A career-spanning documentary directed by actor Michael Rapaport about the hip-hop group A Tribe Called Quest, tracing their start in Queens and their role in the Native Tongues collective. It centers on the strained relationship between members Q-Tip and Phife Dawg, including fraught footage from their 2008 reunion.

A 2023 documentary by Joe Peeler and Rebecca Landsberry-Baker about the Muscogee Nation's press freedom fight. After the tribe repealed its Free Press Act in 2018 and returned its news outlet to the chief and cabinet, veteran reporter Angel Ellis pushes for a constitutional referendum to restore those protections.

Brittany Shyne's American documentary profiles farms in the American South that have been operated for a century. Shot in slow, black-and-white images, it explores the shrinking number of multigenerational Black farmers and why owning land matters to them.

Traces a history of pranks, scandals, and thefts at Walt Disney World, building toward the theft of a nearly half-million-dollar animatronic. Through interviews with members of the park's underground community, it shows how early mischief seemed to inspire later crimes, and turns into a true-crime mystery about who took the figure known as Buzzy.

films.t: Big Star: Nothing Can Hurt Me
films.desc: Drew DeNicola's documentary follows the history of the band Big Star. It explores how the group earned strong critical praise and a devoted cult following despite struggling to achieve commercial success.

films.t: If a Tree Falls: A Story of the Earth Liberation Front
films.desc: Profiles Daniel McGowan, a former member of the Earth Liberation Front who faced life in prison for two arsons against Oregon timber companies. It traces his path from a working-class kid in Queens to eco-activist and weighs environmentalism against terrorism.

A four-part documentary miniseries from 2019, directed by Morgan Neville and Jeff Malmberg, that aired on Showtime. It focuses on the Shangri-La recording studio in Malibu, California, and its owner, producer and Def Jam co-founder Rick Rubin.

An HBO documentary about Bishop Sycamore High School, a fake football program whose nationally televised 2021 game against IMG Academy ended 58-0 and set off a media firestorm. It centers on founder Roy Johnson and the damage his deception caused to young players and their families.
A 2023 American documentary directed by Maren Poitras. It centers on a small group of economists working to change how people think about government debt and what money actually is.

In late 2023, filmmaker Brandon Kramer, a relative, followed the family of Liat Atzili as they worked to free her and her husband after they were taken hostage by Hamas. The documentary shows the family's disagreements over politics and strategy, from her father's criticism of Israel's leadership to others' anger at Hamas and at anti-war protesters.

Alex Stapleton's 2023 documentary traces the life and career of Reggie Jackson, the Hall of Fame baseball player and five-time World Series champion. It also examines his legacy as a pioneering Black athlete, with Jackson talking to other sports stars including Derek Jeter, Bill Russell, and Hank Aaron about race and sports.

Director Yance Ford revisits the violent death of his brother more than two decades earlier. The film examines how silence, race, and fear, combined with the justice system, left his brother's killer free.

Corneliu Porumboiu's documentary follows Laurențiu Ginghină, a provincial civil servant who talks at length with the filmmaker about his ideas for reforming soccer's rules and structure. The conversation drifts from the sport to unrelated subjects such as property disputes, political ideals, and the marks life leaves on people.
Follows an older Minnesota cook whose life is thrown into chaos by a determined filmmaker from Las Vegas, who is set on turning the cook's onion rings into an internationally renowned specialty.

Charlie Shackleton's documentary is about the film he set out to make on the Zodiac Killer before being denied the rights to a former detective's book on the case. Rather than focusing on the killings, it dissects the conventions of true crime storytelling, drawing on well-known examples of the genre.

Follows American defense, intelligence, and elected officials from five presidential administrations, across both parties, as they take part in an improvised simulation of a military-backed coup after a disputed election. The exercise has no script, so the participants must respond to the crisis as it unfolds.

Follows residents of eastern North Carolina, including Elsie Herring, who challenge the large industrial pig farms near their homes and see the stench as a sign of long-standing unfair treatment. Filmed between 2018 and 2022, it shows the community confronting one of the world's most influential meat producers to defend its rights.
Madeleine Gavin's 2023 documentary follows a pastor who uses a covert network to help North Korean families escape and pursue freedom, despite serious risk.
A 2013 documentary tracing cult filmmaker Alejandro Jodorowsky's effort to turn a landmark science fiction novel into a movie, an ambitious undertaking that never reached the screen.

Werner Herzog's 2011 documentary uses intimate interviews with people connected to a Texas death row inmate, along with Herzog's conversations with condemned prisoners about life, death, and their crimes.

An investigative documentary about the underreported problem of sexual assault in the US military and the institutions that allow it to continue. It explores the lasting personal and social harm to service members, focusing on people whose faith in their military service was shattered.

Co-directed by John Maloof and Charlie Siskel, the film follows Maloof's search for the identity of a little-known street photographer whose negatives he bought at an auction. It portrays Maier as a secretive, unconventional woman who worked as a nanny and kept her photography hidden, with her striking images reaching the public only after her death.

Follows Drew Dixon, a former music executive who worked with artists such as Whitney Houston and Method Man, as she weighs whether to publicly accuse hip-hop mogul Russell Simmons of sexual assault. Simmons has denied such allegations. The film presents her as one of the first women of color to speak out about him during the #MeToo era.

A feature documentary shot over 21 years that follows Rabbi Amichai Lau-Lavie, a member of a 38-generation line of Orthodox rabbis, as he struggles with that inherited role and reinvents himself as a drag performer, a queer father, and founder of Lab/Shul, an experimental pop-up congregation. It also examines his efforts to reshape religion and ritual, challenge patriarchy, promote interfaith love, and advocate for peace in Israel and Palestine.

Nathaniel Kahn's 2003 documentary in which he sets out to understand his father, the famous architect Louis Kahn, whom he barely knew. The film visits his father's buildings and speaks with his colleagues, offering a portrait of both the man and his work.

Yasha Levine and Rowan Wernham's documentary examines how Stewart and Lynda Resnick, owners of The Wonderful Company, allegedly gained influence over California's water system during a drought, and how large-scale farming affects the environment. It also suggests that the Resnicks' business interests benefit from continued hostility toward Iran.

A 2026 Netflix documentary directed by Rory Kennedy about chess great Judit Polgar. It follows her childhood as part of a father-led experiment to raise strong chess players, her rise to becoming the youngest grandmaster, and her famous games against Garry Kasparov.

Profiles Ernest Withers, a photographer known for his civil rights-era pictures who also worked as an FBI informant. The film explores both the man behind those well-known photographs and the reasons that may have shaped his choices.

The story of Fanny, a rock band that began as a teenage garage group in 1960s Sacramento and became a pioneering all-women act whose influence was long overlooked. It follows the bandmates as they reunite decades later for a new record deal, mixing archival concert footage with interviews from well-known musicians and discussing the discrimination they faced over race, gender, sexuality, and age.

Kirby Dick's 2009 documentary examines gay and bisexual politicians who hide their sexuality while backing laws that harm LGBT people. It argues that the news media has been reluctant to report on these lawmakers' private lives, unlike comparable stories about straight politicians, and draws on Michael Rogers's work at BlogActive.com.

Filmmaker Penny Lane documents herself preparing to donate a kidney to an unknown recipient, questioning whether the act makes her a good person. Interviews with a bioethicist, a neuroscientist, and a transplant surgeon, along with archival footage of altruistic donors, frame it as a modest study of altruism.

Melinda Maerker's 2023 documentary follows LGBTQ+ families in Midwestern states who face hostility at church, at school, and in their neighborhoods. It also features Minnesota state representative Heather Keeler, a queer mother who is pushing LGBTQ+ rights into politics despite death threats.

An Independent Lens documentary about a first-year alderwoman in Evanston, Illinois, who helped pass the first tax-funded reparations measure in U.S. history for Black Americans. The film also examines the broader national debate over what the country owes for its past.

A satirical documentary that compiles footage from Russian TV channels, including Russia-1, Russia Today, and NTV, showing how they covered Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump during the 2016 election and Trump's first year in office. It presents that coverage as a portrait of modern propaganda and its spread across the world.

Directed by Morgan Neville and Robert Gordon, the film revisits a series of nationally televised debates from 1968 between two prominent public intellectuals: the liberal Gore Vidal and the conservative William F. Buckley Jr.

A 2025 documentary following comedian and podcaster Marc Maron after the sudden death of his partner, filmmaker Lynn Shelton. He candidly examines his mourning, his sense of letdown, and his personal change as he looks for a way forward and tries to turn the loss into material for his comedy.

A 2023 documentary directed by Roy Power and Adam Weiner that follows rock musician Adam Weiner, performing as Low Cut Connie, and his band as they try to stage a concert version of their album for three nights in New York City. Drawing on five years of footage, it mixes intense live performances with the setbacks Weiner faces, which he meets with humor and theatrical flair.

films.t: Love in the Time of Fentanyl
films.desc: A 2022 Canadian documentary directed by Colin Askey that follows a group of people who run a safe injection site in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside neighborhood. It won the Colin Low Award at the 2022 DOXA Documentary Film Festival.

A visually striking documentary that examines China's manufacturing and consumer economy, focusing on the widening gap between rich and poor. It climbs the social ladder from factory workers to middle-class shoppers to the wealthy, showing how each tier depends on the one below it.

Lisa Cortés's documentary, which premiered at Sundance in 2023, portrays the rock pioneer as a man torn between his devout faith and his sexuality and music. It combines archival footage with interviews with fellow musicians and scholars who argue he never received the recognition or money he deserved for helping shape rock 'n' roll.

Looks back at a 1995 Chicago heat wave that killed 739 people in a single week, most of them poor, Black, and elderly. It links that disaster to later natural catastrophes and examines how income, race, and where someone lives shape their odds of surviving such crises, asking why these deaths aren't treated as disasters.

Miranda Yousef's 2023 documentary looks at Thomas Kinkade, the popular artist whose cheerful, mass-produced paintings sold widely in the 1990s. After his death in 2012, his daughters discovered hundreds of private, darker works that revealed a more troubled man, including his struggles with alcohol.

Alexandre O. Philippe's documentary traces how the imagery and cultural influence of The Wizard of Oz recur throughout David Lynch's work, from his early short The Alphabet to Twin Peaks: The Return. Through six perspectives narrated by contemporary voices, it asks whether Lynch's films deepen our understanding of his symbolism and of the 1939 classic's lasting appeal.

A 2022 British documentary drama that follows real men named James Bond around the world, blending interviews, live footage, and re-enactments. It explores how the name and the global Bond franchise shape their identities, fandom, and everyday lives, from a Swedish 007 superfan to a New York theatre director and an ornithologist whose name Ian Fleming borrowed.

Thomas von Steinaecker's documentary examines the career, creative process, and life of filmmaker Werner Herzog, from his early successes to his more recent documentaries. It combines archival and previously unseen footage with interviews with people who have worked with him, including Chloé Zhao, Patti Smith, and Wim Wenders.

films.t: Billy Bragg & Wilco: Man in the Sand
films.desc: A 1999 documentary narrated by Woody Guthrie's daughter Nora that follows British singer-songwriter Billy Bragg as he seeks out the real Woody Guthrie. It traces Guthrie's path from his birthplace in Oklahoma to New York, then covers the making of the Mermaid Avenue albums, which set Guthrie's unpublished lyrics to music with the band Wilco in Dublin.
An HBO documentary directed by Rob Reiner that gives a career overview of Albert Brooks's comedy work, from stand-up to acting, writing, and directing.

Sam Pollard's 2023 documentary traces the rise and struggles of Negro League baseball in the early 20th century. Using rare archival footage and interviews with players such as Satchel Paige, Buck O'Neil, Willie Mays, and Hank Aaron, it examines the league's importance to Black communities and the effects of integration.

Follows activists who block logging roads on Vancouver Island to try to save the old-growth forest in the Fairy Creek valley. Police arrests drew thousands more protesters into a large civil disobedience standoff, and the film also examines the tensions within the movement.

Follows Mats Steen, a Norwegian man with Duchenne muscular dystrophy who spent much of his limited life playing World of Warcraft as a character named Ibelin, forming close friendships with his guild while hiding his identity and illness. Through animated game scenes, recollections from friends and family, and excerpts from his blog, it portrays his life and bonds, up to his death at age 25.

films.ex: A fantastic look at a civil rights movement being born and finding its way. Amazing use of sound and silence to build emotion, and so great that all four leaders were willing/able to be part of it. An excellent movie, one of the best documentaries I've seen in a long time.
films.desc: Revisits an eight-day protest in March 1988, when students at Gallaudet University in Washington, D.C., objected to the appointment of a hearing person as their president and pushed for leadership that reflected the deaf community. Directed by Gallaudet graduate Nyle DiMarco in his directorial debut, it features people who took part describing how they dealt with sexism, ableism, and paternalism, and is narrated in American Sign Language with voiceovers.

A 2025 documentary directed by Lindsay Utz and Michelle Walshe that traces about seven years of Jacinda Ardern's life, from her sudden rise to New Zealand's top political job in 2017 to her surprise resignation in early 2023. It combines home videos shot by her husband, audio recordings of her own interviews from her time in office, and newer interviews to examine her leadership through major crises and the wider strain on democracy and public trust.

films.ex: This wouldn't have worked if Wells wasn't the suavest motherfucker of all time. But he is, so it did, except for the interlude near the end that is basically just his hot Croatian girlfriend getting progressively more naked. But he still manages to bring the shaggy dog story about Picasso to a…
films.desc: Orson Welles's 1973 film is an unconventional documentary about deception. It follows art forger Elmyr de Hory and his biographer Clifford Irving, who also produced a fake Howard Hughes autobiography, then turns to Hughes himself and to Welles's own early career, with some playful deceptions of Welles's own along the way.

films.ex: You know what's going to happen from the first frame but that doesn't make it any less devastating when it happens. An amazing filmmaking feat that should get nominated for Oscars for sound and editing.
films.desc: Uses police bodycam recordings from many home visits to show a close-knit neighborhood dealing with one resident who keeps harassing her neighbors. Her behavior eventually turns dangerous when it leads to a deadly crime.

The 2012 entry in the Up Series, which revisits a group of English people every seven years, starting with Seven Up in 1964. At age 56, the participants, first interviewed as children from diverse backgrounds, discuss major life changes and unexpected developments.

Directed by Oscar-winning filmmaker Ben Proudfoot, the film follows 93-year-old Chris Hesse, once Kwame Nkrumah's personal cinematographer. Losing his sight, Hesse works to recover and bring home more than 1,000 films from the 1950s and 1960s that document Africa's independence era, footage that has never been shown publicly.

A 2025 documentary by Laura Poitras and Mark Obenhaus that profiles journalist Seymour Hersh. It follows his decades of exposing hidden wrongdoing, from the My Lai massacre to Abu Ghraib, and also covers his personal background and some of his errors.

A five-part Apple TV+ documentary series about filmmaker Martin Scorsese, tracing how his personal experiences shaped his films from his early NYU student work to the present. It includes interviews with collaborators such as Steven Spielberg and Robert De Niro, his family, and Scorsese himself, along with access to his private archives.

Directed by Colin Hanks, this 2025 documentary remembers Canadian comedian John Candy through rare archival footage, photos, and interviews with people who knew him well, who recount his life and career and portray him as a kind, gifted performer.

Examines an unsuccessful 2020 effort to oust Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, led by former U.S. Green Beret Jordan Goudreau. Using interviews, archival footage, and personal stories, it explores Goudreau's motives and the role of hired fighters, while showing how conflicting accounts make the truth hard to pin down and how the operation affected the people involved.

films.t: Watch the Sound with Mark Ronson
films.desc: A six-part Apple TV+ documentary series, hosted by Mark Ronson, that looks at how technology has shaped the way music is made. Ronson talks with artists and producers, including Paul McCartney and Questlove, and composes a new piece of music at the end of each episode.

Rob Epstein's 1984 documentary traces Harvey Milk's life, from his grassroots activism to his 1977 election as California's first openly gay elected official on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors. Drawing on television footage and interviews, it ends with his 1978 assassination and serves as a record of 1970s San Francisco, where social liberalization and widespread anti-gay hostility existed side by side.

Raoul Peck's 2016 documentary relies entirely on James Baldwin's recorded public appearances and his unfinished final manuscript, narrated by Samuel L. Jackson. Using the assassinations of Malcolm X, Martin Luther King Jr., and Medgar Evers as its starting point, it examines how American society constructs and maintains a distorted image of Black people.

Ava DuVernay's 2016 documentary examines how race, the justice system, and the mass imprisonment of Americans are connected. It argues that the exception in the Thirteenth Amendment, which allows forced labor as punishment for crime, has let slavery-like practices continue through the prison system and the businesses that profit from it.

Barbara Kopple's 1976 documentary follows Kentucky coal miners who walked off the job in 1973 after Eastover Mining Company refused to sign their labor agreement, offering a detailed portrait of the workers' struggle during the strike.

films.t: When the Levees Broke: A Requiem in Four Acts
films.desc: Spike Lee's 2006 HBO documentary traces the destruction New Orleans suffered when its levees gave way during Hurricane Katrina. Using archival clips, photographs, and interviews with officials, engineers, and residents, it portrays people grieving and struggling to survive while arguing that the flooding was preventable and made worse by government failures.

A 1982 wordless documentary directed by Godfrey Reggio with a score by Philip Glass, juxtaposing American natural landscapes with busy cityscapes to suggest a society that has lost its equilibrium. Cinematographer Ron Fricke shot largely unscripted footage across several years using slow motion and time-lapse, assembled into an 86-minute film set to the music.

Claude Nuridsany and Marie Perennou's 1996 documentary follows the insects and other small creatures of a meadow through a summer day, a night, and the next dawn. Filmed at close range, it presents the grass and its dewdrops as a vast, unfamiliar landscape, where one day spans what would be a whole season for these short-lived animals.

Marc Singer's 2000 American documentary follows people who live in a disused part of New York City's subway system, known as the Freedom Tunnel, tracking this small underground community in that abandoned space.
Michael Apted's 1977 British documentary revisits the same group of fourteen people from different social backgrounds, now young adults, whom he first filmed at age seven.

Spike Lee's 1997 documentary traces the people and circumstances behind the bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama, during the height of the civil rights movement. The attack killed four young African-American girls.

A 1995 documentary by Rob Epstein and Jeffrey Friedman that traces how gay characters have appeared in Hollywood films, from subtle coded figures to harmful caricatures and, later, more candid portrayals. Narrated by Lily Tomlin, with interviews with actors such as Tom Hanks and Susan Sarandon, it examines how movies have both reflected and warped the way queer people appear on screen.

films.t: I'll Be Gone in the Dark
films.desc: A six-part HBO documentary series directed by Liz Garbus that traces the crimes of the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, who is alleged to have committed at least a dozen murders and fifty rapes over two decades. It also follows journalist Michelle McNamara, who spent her last years obsessively trying to track him down.

Tia Lessin and Carl Deal's 2008 documentary about a young couple who survive Hurricane Katrina and confront their troubled past in the storm's aftermath. It is built largely from camera footage Kimberly Rivers Roberts shot as she and her neighbors waited out the storm in a New Orleans attic, mixed with news archives and home videos, and it examines race, class, and the government's responsibility to its citizens.

Errol Morris's 1997 documentary follows four men with unusual obsessions: a lion tamer, a topiary gardener, a hairless mole-rat expert, and an MIT robotics designer. Morris interviews them face-to-camera and mixes in varied film formats and archival clips to connect their pursuits into a reflection on human ambition and the future.

A 2006 BBC nature documentary miniseries, narrated in its original version by David Attenborough, that tours the world's major habitats across eleven episodes. Each episode focuses on a different environment, such as polar regions, mountains, deserts, jungles, and the deep ocean, showing the wildlife that lives in them.

A documentary series tracing the career of O.J. Simpson, from his peak to his downfall. It argues that his highly publicized murder trial revealed deep divisions in American society along racial lines.

A 10-part documentary series revisiting the Chicago Bulls' final championship season with Michael Jordan, using previously unseen footage from that year. It aired in weekly two-episode installments in spring 2020 and profiles Jordan's teammates and coach Phil Jackson.

Martin Bell's 1984 documentary, made with photographer Mary Ellen Mark and journalist Cheryl McCall, follows young people living on the streets of Seattle in 1983. It shows how they scrape by through hustling, begging, and scavenging after leaving troubled homes.

A 2014 American documentary series hosted by astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson, serving as a modern successor to Carl Sagan's 1980 series. Using computer animation and a fictional flying vessel as a storytelling device, it traces scientific discoveries about the universe, from the Big Bang and the age of the cosmos to the origins of life and humanity's place within it.

A 1992 documentary directed by Ron Fricke, made from striking footage shot around the world. It moves from religious rituals and natural splendor to harsher scenes of industrial production and poverty, and has no spoken dialogue.

Follows two Black teenagers from inner-city Chicago, William Gates and Arthur Agee, as they commute to a predominantly white suburban high school on basketball scholarships, filmed over five years. It tracks their pursuit of NBA careers and the pressures they face from their families, schools, and dreams.

films.t: The Jinx: The Life and Deaths of Robert Durst
films.desc: A 2015 six-part documentary series directed by Andrew Jarecki and produced and shot by Marc Smerling about their seven-year investigation into several unsolved crimes linked to Robert Durst, a member of the New York billionaire Durst family, who cooperated with the filmmakers and maintained his innocence.

Chris Smith's 1999 documentary about Mark Borchardt, a Wisconsin filmmaker trying to finish his independent movie with help from his mother, his elderly uncle, and local friends. It also captures the money troubles and personal strain that come with chasing that goal, and is presented as a portrait of ambition and the American Dream.

Morgan Neville's 2018 documentary about Fred Rogers, host of the children's program Mister Rogers' Neighborhood. Using interviews and archival footage, it portrays his empathy, his kindness toward people of all ages and backgrounds, and his talent for making viewers feel less alone.

Terry Zwigoff's 1994 documentary follows the life of Robert Crumb, a pioneering underground comic artist best known for creating Fritz the Cat. It portrays Crumb as an eccentric man who is both likable and unsettling, and whose art has drawn attention for more than thirty years.
A 2004 travel documentary in which actors Ewan McGregor and Charley Boorman ride motorcycles roughly 20,000 miles across 12 countries in 115 days. It is the first installment of the Long Way series.

Werner Herzog's 2005 documentary about Timothy Treadwell, a bear enthusiast who spent years living among brown bears in Alaska's Katmai National Park. Built from Treadwell's own footage and interviews with friends and experts, it also covers his fatal 2003 bear attack alongside his girlfriend, Amie Huguenard, and Herzog's view that Treadwell's romantic idea of nature led him to underestimate the danger.

Peter Jackson's 2018 documentary presents the First World War through archival footage from the Imperial War Museums, paired with BBC audio of veterans recounting their experiences. The footage has been colourised, converted to 3D, and enhanced with modern techniques to show life at the front in new detail.

films.t: Paradise Lost: The Child Murders at Robin Hood Hills
films.desc: Joe Berlinger and Bruce Sinofsky's 1996 documentary about the 1993 killings of three young boys in West Memphis, Arkansas, and the conviction of three teenagers for them. It combines courtroom footage, access to judges' chambers, and interviews with both the victims' and the accused's families to show a small town struggling with animosity, vengeance, and punishment while the question of guilt remains open.

A documentary about the 2018 effort to rescue twelve Thai boys and their coach, who became stranded in a cave system after floodwaters rose. Directed by Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, it was released in 2021 by National Geographic.

Follows Leon Gast, who went to Africa in 1974 to film a music festival held alongside the Muhammad Ali and George Foreman heavyweight title fight. It mostly shows Ali training and enjoying his role in postcolonial Africa, with interviews with Norman Mailer and George Plimpton about the fight's impact.

Errol Morris's 1988 documentary examines the case of Randall Adams, who was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1976 killing of a Dallas police officer. It mixes dramatized reenactments, interviews, and a Philip Glass score to reinvestigate the crime, and is credited with helping overturn Adams's conviction.

films.ex: Watching this with someone who has a fear of heights is a kinetic experience. I wrote that sentence and I have no idea what it actually means. Anyway, this movie is literally breathtaking.
films.desc: Follows Alex Honnold, a climber who trains to scale El Capitan in Yosemite without ropes or safety equipment. As he prepares, injuries and a new relationship make the risk feel even greater.

films.ex: I hate it when the word "inspirational" is attached to stories about people with disabilities, but this really was inspirational. Sometimes the hippies did good things.
films.desc: Follows a group of disabled teenagers at a rundown summer camp near Woodstock in the early 1970s, where their experiences sparked a movement that changed their lives. Directed by Jim LeBrecht and Nicole Newnham, with LeBrecht and disability rights activist Judith Heumann appearing as subjects.

films.t: The King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters
films.desc: Follows rival players chasing world records on classic arcade games, with the contest for the top Donkey Kong score at the center. A small-stakes competition played with real intensity.

Dave Grohl's directing debut traces the Los Angeles recording studio Sound City from its 1969 opening to its 2011 closing as a commercial studio. It focuses on the albums made there and on its prized Neve mixing console, which Grohl later bought.

Looks into Sixto Rodriguez, a Detroit singer-songwriter whose two late-1960s albums flopped at home. Two South African fans, whose country had quietly embraced his music during apartheid, set out to learn what became of him.

Celebrates the Los Angeles session musicians who played on a large share of 1960s and 1970s hits for artists such as Frank Sinatra and the Beach Boys. It argues that they have never been credited as much as they deserve.

Follows Tim Wakefield of the Red Sox and R.A. Dickey of the Mets through the 2011 season as both rely on the knuckleball, a pitch that is hard to control and often doubted. Retired knuckleballers and other baseball figures also appear.

Ken Burns's 1994 PBS miniseries on the history of baseball, built like a nine-inning game with an inning for each era. It ties the sport to larger events in American life, and a later Tenth Inning carried it through 2009.

Tells the story of the Portland Mavericks, an independent baseball team Bing Russell started in 1973 with no major-league affiliation. It covers the open tryouts, big crowds and unconventional players and staff, including Kurt Russell.

Jennie Livingston's 1990 film follows the New York drag ball scene and the people who developed voguing. It shows how those gatherings gave a community pride, belonging and a place for glamour and dreams.

A two-part Paramount+ documentary on how MP3s and online chat rooms led to widespread free trading of copyrighted music around the industry's 1999 peak. It also follows a man who smuggled CDs out of a pressing plant before their release dates.

Follows Matt Green as he walks every street of New York City, more than 8,000 miles over several years. Director Jeremy Workman joins part of the walk, and the film focuses on the people Green meets along the way.
More than a hundred comedians riff on a famously filthy joke that comics have passed around for generations. Each puts a personal spin on it, showing how timing and style shape the telling.

James Marsh's account of Philippe Petit, the French high-wire artist who secretly strung a cable between the World Trade Center towers in 1974 and walked across it. It tells the illegal stunt as a suspenseful heist story.

Michael Moore uses the Columbine High School shooting as a starting point to look at gun violence and the fear he sees in American culture. He interviews survivors, Charlton Heston, Marilyn Manson and others. It won the Oscar for Best Documentary.

Robert Kenner's film argues that a few large corporations dominate U.S. food production. It says industrial methods of raising livestock and growing crops harm health, animals, workers, farmers and the environment.

Michael Moore's 2004 film is a sharp critique of George W. Bush and his administration. It looks at the events leading up to the September 11 attacks and the U.S. move toward war, and suggests that oil interests played a part.
Morgan Spurlock looks at how the fast food industry shapes what people eat. To see the effect himself, he eats only McDonald's meals for a month and tracks what happens to his health.

Michael Wadleigh's 1970 film follows the 1969 Woodstock festival in Bethel, New York, from setup to cleanup. It mixes concert footage with portraits of the crowd and the festival's troubles, such as fences falling and drug use.

Bruce Brown's 1971 film about motorcycle racing in the U.S. and abroad, from road racing to motocross, ice racing and desert events. Riders such as Mert Lawwill, Steve McQueen and Malcolm Smith appear.

Combines early-1930s footage shot by Michael Leahy with interviews made about fifty years later with the surviving brothers and some of the highlanders. It covers the Australian prospectors who went looking for gold in New Guinea's highlands and found thousands of people who had never seen outsiders.

A roughly fourteen-hour PBS series on the American civil rights movement, created by Henry Hampton. It uses archival footage, photographs and interviews with both supporters and opponents of the movement.

films.t: Hôtel Terminus: The Life and Times of Klaus Barbie
films.desc: Marcel Ophuls's nearly four-and-a-half-hour film about Klaus Barbie, the Nazi officer known for his time in Lyon. It builds a picture of Barbie and his era from interviews and testimony, organized in loosely structured parts.
Bruce Weber's black-and-white 1988 portrait of jazz trumpeter Chet Baker. Fans, bandmates, ex-wives and children recall a career that began in the 1950s and was later marked by heroin addiction.

Al Reinert's 1989 film edits original NASA footage from the Apollo missions into what feels like a single trip to the Moon. The narration comes from interviews with Apollo astronauts, and Brian Eno wrote the score.
Barbara Kopple's 1990 film follows a mid-1980s strike by Hormel meatpacking workers in Austin, Minnesota. It shows the hardships of the strikers and the tensions among their union leaders.

Mark Kitchell's film on the 1960s protest movements in Berkeley and the Bay Area, from the 1960 HUAC hearings through the Free Speech Movement, antiwar protest and the 1969 People's Park clash. It pairs archival footage with interviews with former activists.

Chris Hegedus and D. A. Pennebaker follow Bill Clinton's 1992 presidential campaign, centered on strategists James Carville and George Stephanopoulos in Little Rock. It covers the primaries, the debates and the campaign's fights over media coverage.

About the 1958 photo shoot in Harlem where a large crowd of top jazz musicians turned up for what became a famous group portrait. The hour-long film uses archival performances, home-movie footage and interviews with surviving participants and the photographer.

A 1996 PBS American Experience film on the clash between Orson Welles and publisher William Randolph Hearst over Citizen Kane. It uses interviews with people who knew both men to show how Hearst's side tried to suppress the film.

Revisits the 1993 deadly events near Waco, Texas, which left four federal agents and 76 Branch Davidians dead. The film argues that the ATF may have pushed the confrontation toward violence more than is usually acknowledged.

Kevin Macdonald's 1999 film on the 1972 Munich Olympics attack, in which militants killed eleven Israeli athletes. Using interviews, archival footage and narration by Michael Douglas, it argues that the German rescue effort was badly planned and carried out.

Ry Cooder gathers aging Cuban musicians in Havana to record an album of traditional music, and the film follows them to concerts in Amsterdam and New York. Wim Wenders mixes the performances with interviews and footage of Cuba today.

Follows Paul Pena, a blind blues musician who heard Tuvan throat singing on shortwave radio and taught himself the language to study it. The film follows his trip to Tuva, where he performed with a well-known local singer.
Michael Moore's 1989 film about his hometown of Flint, Michigan, as General Motors cuts jobs and the city declines. Moore keeps trying to get GM chairman Roger Smith to come and see the damage.
Follows eight young contestants as they prepare for and compete in the 1999 National Spelling Bee in Washington, DC. It shows their varied backgrounds and what the contest means to them.

Andrew Jarecki's 2003 film about the Friedmans, a family that seems ordinary from outside until the father and youngest son are arrested and charged with serious crimes. This summary is based on a short synopsis, so details of the case are not covered here.
Luc Jacquet's 2005 French nature documentary follows emperor penguins as they cross the frozen Antarctic each winter to reach their breeding grounds, a journey made for thousands of years.
Follows quadriplegic athletes who play wheelchair rugby, a full-contact sport, as they head toward the Paralympics in Athens. It shows the physical and personal challenges they face.
Follows Al Gore as he works to persuade people worldwide that climate change is a serious and well-supported threat. This summary is based on a short synopsis.

Banksy directs this 2009 film about Thierry Guetta, a French shop owner who tries to film the street art scene and its best-known artists. Banksy would not be filmed by Guetta, which shapes the film's focus.

Josh Fox's first-person film on the spread of hydraulic fracturing for natural gas in the U.S. After a drilling company offers to lease his rural property, he visits residents in several states who describe contaminated water and illness they link to the drilling.

Judith Helfand begins by looking for safer siding for her parents' Long Island home. She ends up investigating the health and environmental hazards of PVC plastic, including affected communities in Louisiana and Venice, Italy.

Susan Saladoff revisits the well-known case of an elderly Albuquerque woman who sued McDonald's over a coffee spill, asking what actually happened. It also looks at how the media, politicians and business groups used the case to shape views of lawsuits, damage caps and arbitration.
A Morgan Neville film about the backup singers behind major popular musicians who seldom get public credit. It looks at the conflicts, sacrifices and rewards of their careers.

Laura Poitras's film records her and journalist Glenn Greenwald meeting NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden in Hong Kong in June 2013. It shows how contact began through anonymous encrypted emails and how Snowden shared documents on government surveillance.

Bryan Fogel set out to show that athletes could dope without being caught. His adviser, Moscow anti-doping lab head Grigory Rodchenkov, then became a whistleblower on a Russian state doping program, and the film became an exposé of it.

A Chinese billionaire opens a factory in a closed General Motors plant in Ohio and hires about 2,000 local workers. Early hope turns to friction as the company's methods clash with American working-class expectations.
Craig Foster swims daily in cold waters at the southern tip of Africa and forms a close bond with a wild octopus. The film pairs underwater footage with his reflective narration.

films.t: Summer of Soul (...Or, When the Revolution Could Not Be Televised)
films.desc: Questlove's first feature as director, built on concert footage of a major celebration of Black music, culture and style. It suggests music can help people heal in turbulent times.
Follows Alexei Navalny after he survived poisoning with a nerve toxin in August 2020. During his long recovery he learns troubling details about the attack and decides to go back home.

films.ex: Fascinating
films.desc: Follows musician and opposition leader Bobi Wine during Uganda's 2021 presidential election as he rallies supporters against a government that has held power for about 35 years. It shows the dangers he and his followers face.

Errol Morris's 1978 film about people connected to pet cemeteries, including owners and embalmers, who talk about their work, their losses and their feelings. It grew out of a news item about hundreds of animal remains being moved.
Jonathan Demme's concert film of Talking Heads performing over three nights in December 1983 at the Pantages Theater in Hollywood, on their tour for Speaking in Tongues.

Gabriela Cowperthwaite's film centers on Tilikum, a killer whale linked to three deaths, one of them a senior trainer. It examines the harm that can follow when highly intelligent animals are kept in captivity.

Peter Jackson's three-part series revisits the Beatles' making of Let It Be in early 1969, using unseen film and about 140 hours of session audio. It includes their final live performance on the rooftop of Apple's building in London.

Charles Ferguson's film, narrated by Matt Damon, examines the causes of the 2008 financial crisis. It uses interviews with financial insiders, politicians and journalists to show how the industry grew unchecked and how its ties to government and regulators mattered.

Follows photographer James Nachtwey for two years as he covers conflicts such as those in Indonesia, Kosovo and Palestine. It looks at why he does the work and how he goes about it, using tiny cameras attached to his own.
A 1992 documentary on the history of cinematography. Working cinematographers and filmmakers discuss iconic shots, the films that inspired them and why camera work matters.

Errol Morris's 2003 film centers on Robert McNamara, Secretary of Defense under Kennedy and Johnson and later head of the World Bank. McNamara reflects on major 20th-century events in a long interview, mixed with archival footage and a Philip Glass score.
Errol Morris's 1991 film on cosmologist Stephen Hawking. It combines his theories about the universe with his personal story, with contributions from physicist Kip Thorne.

Errol Morris interviewed former Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld for 33 hours. The film looks at his career through the memos he wrote, including the Iraq War and detainee policy, and at his evasive answers.

films.t: This Is a Robbery: The World's Biggest Art Heist
films.desc: A 2021 Netflix series on the 1990 theft of art from a Boston museum by two men posing as police, which has never been solved. Across four episodes it looks at the cold case and a wider conspiracy said to involve criminal groups in several countries.

Ursula Liang's film on the death of Akai Gurley, a young Black man killed in a dark stairwell by Peter Liang, a Chinese American rookie NYPD officer. It uses the case to challenge simple assumptions about racism in policing and follows the difficult road to accountability.

Dziga Vertov's 1929 Soviet film is a fast montage of a city's daily life, its people at work and at play and the machines that keep it running. It uses split screens, slow motion and freeze-frames to make an experimental portrait of filmmaking itself.

Chris Wilcha secretly filmed his time working for the Columbia Record and Tape Club, where he was hired to start a niche-marketing division. The film looks at how alternative music is packaged and sold once big business takes it on.
Songs From the Hole is a documentary that details the life in prison of James "JJ'88" Jacobs, a man convicted of murder as a teenager and how he became a musician while in prison.

Thirty-four days before she's sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss.
